notation.meaning: Supply of college and non-college labor in efficiency units
Elasticity of substitution between the two types
Estimated elasticity of substitution in the example

blocks.md: **Estimating the canonical model on 1963–2017 US data gives $\hat\sigma \approx 2.3$ (OLS) to $2.6$ (2SLS): college and non-college workers are substitutes, with $\sigma$ comfortably above 1.**

2SLS instruments relative supply with the relative log population of college to non-college ([Instrumental Variables and 2SLS](note:instrumental-variables-and-2sls)). The implied $\sigma = -1/\hat\beta$ is computed from unrounded coefficients, so $1/0.44 = 2.27$ shows as 2.28.

- The trend is 0.0178 a year in log-wage units. Multiplying by $\sigma$ converts it to relative **demand** growth: about $2.28 \times 0.0178 \approx 4\%$ a year.
- Since $\sigma > 1$, skill-augmenting technology **raises** the premium ([Factor-Augmenting Technology](note:factor-augmenting-technology)).
Katz and Murphy (1992), on 1963–87 data, estimated $\sigma \approx 1.4$. (From the literature, not this lecture.)
